extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in comedy, pop culture, and #MeToo-era debates (general Refinery29 audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing live stand-up comedy sets for how performers handle #MeToo-era topics, audience interaction, venue context, and the ethical/creative lines of offensive material; based on five nights at NYC venues Comedy Cellar/Village Underground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punching up, not down
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes should target powerful or deserving subjects (punch up) rather than attack already-marginalized people (punch down).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer highlights relief when a joke "punched up, not down" (Sam Morril). Young comics who place punchlines thoughtfully get louder laughs; older comics relying on punching down divide the room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reframe material in light of #MeToo
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians should question and, when appropriate, rework material that might be insensitive given the cultural moment and revelations about sexual misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece asks whether #MeToo changed how comedians joked about sex and dating and notes it often wasn’t evident that older comics paused to reframe their material; younger comics appeared more thoughtful and updated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat survivors and sexual violence with care
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid jokes that trivialize sexual assault, cast doubt on survivors, or use survivors' pain as a punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of problematic material include jokes casting doubt on women who came forward based on appearance, and repeated rape-related jokes (Bill Cosby references). The article contrasts this with comics who place such material responsibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect audience feedback; don't blame them for failed jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: When material doesn't land, performers should adapt rather than accuse the audience of being 'too uptight' or 'not game enough.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older comedians routinely turned on the audience for not laughing; the writer labels this an anti-pattern and praises comics who adjusted or whose controversial bits were constructed to land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match material to venue/time/context
rubrics_metrics.description: Select jokes appropriate to the show’s time, venue, and typical audience (e.g., brunch shows are tamer than late-night 11:30 p.m. sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brunch audiences responded differently than late-night crowds; late hours often produce more unfiltered, outlandish material at the Cellar and Underground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not single out or publicly shame audience members
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid calling out individual audience members—especially marginalized attendees—for not laughing or for their identity/choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author was publicly criticized for not laughing and was asked if she would "go home and blog about this." Such targeted shaming contributes to an unsafe environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid slurs and explicitly demeaning language
rubrics_metrics.description: Using slurs or demeaning epithets (e.g., repeatedly calling the crowd "fags") is unacceptable and can silence or alienate the room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comic who used slurs and political provocation was met with silence and left the stage to no applause; this demonstrates social and performative consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider accountability and whether to address personal controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics facing allegations should weigh acknowledging misconduct; ignoring admissions can shape audience reaction and moral calculus around a comeback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Louis C.K. reportedly returned without addressing admitted sexual misconduct; the audience response (standing ovation for one reported appearance) and ensuing backlash illustrate the stakes of not addressing controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize audience safety and comfort
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy should not create an environment where audience members—especially those from marginalized groups—feel unsafe or unwelcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author felt unsafe when fellow patrons minimized sexual-assault concerns; a performance culture that rewards or normalizes such minimization harms attendee wellbeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make space for diverse, younger voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Bookers and venues should create opportunities for younger and more diverse comedians, whose material may better reflect current norms and draw stronger responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer notes louder laughs for younger, diverse, thoughtful comics but observes the Cellar doesn’t make as much room for them, even though comedy beyond those venues is flourishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical humor can avoid personal controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics may safely riff on topical controversies in general while choosing not to address their own allegations, but this choice affects tone and audience perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aziz Ansari avoided addressing the allegation reported about him and instead riffed on unrelated controversies; his low-energy, workmanlike set prompted mixed feelings in the writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shock value versus thoughtful craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying solely on shock or offensiveness is different from constructing thoughtful material that engages controversial topics responsibly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older comics often default to outlandish/offensive shock bits that divide the room; younger comics tended toward material described as diverse and thoughtful and were better received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Club policies and stage rules (recording/heckling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect venue-specific rules such as prohibitions on recording or note-taking and house policies on heckling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Cellar forbids recording and taking notes; waitstaff enforced a no-heckling rule during a show where a woman shouted at a comic and was told heckling wasn't allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience composition influences norms and tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: The demographic makeup of a crowd (tourists vs. locals, gender balance, political leanings) affects which comics and jokes are welcomed or rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Cellar’s audience was described as almost exclusively out-of-towners and at times an 'emerging army of allies' for offensive comics, shaping an atmosphere that could normalize harmful material.
